name: Paracetamol
indications: Moderate to severe pain (adjunct with opioids via IV/PO)
clinicalNote: JRCALC & NHS staple. Always check cumulative 24-hour intake (including over-the-counter cold remedies like Lemsip or Co-codamol) before administering to prevent hepatotoxicity.

name: Salbutamol
indications: Wheeze associated with anaphylaxis or smoke inhalation
clinicalNote: Nebulised oxygen-driven in acute asthma (6–8 L/min); in COPD, limit oxygen-driven nebulisation to 6 minutes to minimize hypercapnic respiratory acidosis risk.

name: Ipratropium Bromide
indications: Moderate to life-threatening acute asthma (with Salbutamol)
Acute exacerbation of COPD unresponsive to initial SABA
clinicalNote: Blocks vagally mediated bronchoconstriction. Single 500 microgram nebulised dose in pre-hospital emergency care per JRCALC guidelines.

name: Furosemide
clinicalNote: UK rINN name (formerly Frusemide). Inhibits Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the ascending loop of Henle; also produces early venodilation in acute pulmonary oedema.

name: Ondansetron
indications: Prevention and treatment of nausea and vomiting
clinicalNote: Administer IV slowly over at least 2–3 minutes (or IM). Contraindicated in congenital long QT syndrome.

name: Atorvastatin
indications: Primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
clinicalNote: The single most dispensed medication in England. On history taking, its presence indicates cardiovascular risk profile or prior vascular event.

name: Amlodipine
indications: Prophylaxis of chronic stable and Prinzmetal's angina
clinicalNote: Causes peripheral arterial vasodilation. Commonly causes ankle oedema (which does not respond to diuretics) and can contribute to postural hypotension in older patients.

name: Lansoprazole
indications: Gastric protection alongside NSAID or antiplatelet therapy
clinicalNote: Suppresses gastric acid secretion by inhibiting the H+/K+ ATPase pump in gastric parietal cells.

name: Ramipril
clinicalNote: Pre-hospital pearls: well-known cause of persistent dry cough and non-histaminergic bradykinin-mediated angioedema (often affecting lips/tongue without urticaria).

name: Omeprazole
clinicalNote: Frequently prescribed alongside Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) or DOACs to reduce upper GI bleeding risk.

name: Bisoprolol
clinicalNote: Important during trauma or sepsis assessment: blunts physiological compensatory tachycardia, potentially masking early hypovolaemic or septic shock.

name: Apixaban
indications: Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation
Treatment and prophylaxis of DVT and pulmonary embolism
clinicalNote: Critical red flag in head injury / silver trauma: patients on DOACs require hospital assessment after head injury per NICE & JRCALC guidelines even if GCS is 15.

name: Metformin
clinicalNote: Increases insulin sensitivity without stimulating insulin secretion (rarely causes hypoglycaemia alone). Risk of lactic acidosis in severe dehydration, sepsis, or acute kidney injury.

name: Adrenaline
clinicalNote: UK BNF/rINN prefers Adrenaline (Epinephrine). Always double-check concentration: 1:1,000 (1mg/1mL) for IM anaphylaxis vs 1:10,000 (1mg/10mL) for IV/IO cardiac arrest.

name: Glyceryl Trinitrate
indications: Acute coronary syndrome / ischaemic cardiac chest pain
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (when systolic BP > 110 mmHg)
clinicalNote: Commonly abbreviated GTN. Contraindicated in hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg), severe aortic stenosis, and recent PDE-5 inhibitor use (e.g., Sildenafil, Tadalafil).

name: Chlorphenamine
indications: Symptomatic relief of allergy and urticaria
Adjunct after initial resuscitation in anaphylaxis
clinicalNote: UK rINN name (formerly Chlorpheniramine / Piriton). Second-line symptom control after Adrenaline in allergic reactions.

name: Tranexamic Acid
indications: Major trauma with actual or suspected severe haemorrhage
Moderate to severe traumatic brain injury (within 3 hours)
clinicalNote: Inhibits plasminogen activation to stabilize blood clots. Must be administered within 3 hours of injury (1g IV over 10 minutes in adults).

name: Amiodarone
indications: Shock-refractory VF / pulseless VT (after 3rd and 5th shocks)
clinicalNote: Prolongs phase 3 repolarisation of the cardiac action potential. Administered as 300mg IV/IO bolus after 3rd shock, and 150mg after 5th shock in ALS.

name: Levothyroxine
clinicalNote: Among the top 5 most prescribed NHS community medications. Long half-life (~7 days); non-adherence over weeks can precipitate hypothermia and bradycardia.

name: Clopidogrel
indications: Secondary prevention post-TIA or ischaemic stroke
Acute coronary syndrome / PCI stenting (with Aspirin)
clinicalNote: Irreversibly inhibits platelet aggregation for the lifespan of the platelet (7–10 days). Increases bleeding risk in trauma.
